description: We are a driven team from American Space Dushanbe competing in our first hackathon with one goal: winning! Passionate about space exploration, we are building an interactive space mission design game about journeying into space. Our squad combines strong coding, backend/API integration, storytelling, and pitching to turn our concept into a standout project. Our roster is already full—we aren’t looking for new members, just excited to build, innovate, and connect!
summary:
LUNARVERSE is a story-driven space mission game that turns real NASA data into playable science. Players join the fictional AURORA-1 expedition to Kepler-452 b, a super-Earth in its star’s habitable zone, using parameters from the NASA Exoplanet Archive and Jenkins et al. (2015): radius, orbital period and orbital distance.

Players make mission decisions, face uncertainty and a crisis, and learn how astronomers actually detect planets through the transit method. Kepler-452 b is a Confirmed Planet that the Archive also flags as Controversial. We make that uncertainty part of gameplay, so players learn to separate observations, calculations, hypotheses and fiction. The question shifts from “What did scientists find?” to “How do we know?”

The game needs no prior knowledge of astronomy and is built for beginners and for regions with limited access to science resources. Stylized cel-shaded 3D graphics, built in Godot, clearly separate artistic vision from scientific imagery.

Our goal is to help players develop scientific thinking, introduce them to open NASA data, and spark curiosity about real space exploration, so they leave wanting to open the NASA Exoplanet Archive themselves.
details:
LUNARVERSE: The Last Signal

Project Justification: Scientific Value, Social Impact, NASA Data, Inclusivity NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Challenge: Space Mission Design Game

Items in [brackets] are details only the team can confirm. Fill them in or delete them before submitting. Nothing in this document should describe a feature that is not in the submitted build.

1. Project Overview

LUNARVERSE: The Last Signal is a story-driven 3D space mission game that combines interactive storytelling, real NASA exoplanet data and science education. Players lead the fictional AURORA-1 expedition to Kepler-452 b, a real planet discovered by NASA's Kepler mission. They make mission decisions, work with limited resources, face uncertainty, and gradually discover the science behind real space exploration.

The project rests on one idea: science should not be reserved for people with special training, laboratory access or technical backgrounds.

Humanity now receives enormous amounts of information about the universe from space telescopes and missions, and NASA makes much of that data public. Yet a wide gap remains between data being available and data being understood. Someone may hear about an exoplanet discovery, see an illustration and read a few numbers, but still not understand how scientists obtained them, or why small differences in a measurement can matter enormously.

LUNARVERSE aims to close that gap. Instead of presenting science as tables, graphs and dense explanations, it places the player inside a mission where scientific facts shape the choices they face. The data is not decoration. It is the intellectual foundation of the game: it sets the context of the expedition, explains the target object, and shows how real observations become knowledge and hypotheses.

Our goal is simple: we don't just want people to look at space, we want them to start thinking like explorers.

2. The Problem We Want to Solve

2.1 The gap between discovery and public understanding

Space science moves fast. Every year brings new exoplanet catalogs, new observations and new papers. But this information is usually published for specialists. For most people, terms such as transit method, orbital period, planet radius and statistical confidence are abstract and hard to connect to anything familiar.

This creates a paradox: more open scientific data exists than ever before, yet much of the potential audience cannot meaningfully engage with it. We believe the issue is not only that science is complex, but that there are too few accessible ways to experience it.

LUNARVERSE offers a different approach: explain scientific ideas through events, decisions, consequences and visual interaction. For example, rather than just telling players that Kepler-452 b has an orbital period of about 384.8 Earth days, the game can show how that number relates to the planet's motion around its star, to how long observations must last, and to how a mission would be planned.

2.2 Limited youth engagement with real science

Many young people love space, science fiction, games and technology, but do not see how those interests connect to real science. Video games already hold their attention, and they let people explore, experiment and see the consequences of their actions. LUNARVERSE uses that existing interest as an entry point to STEM. Instead of saying "study astronomy," it invites the player on an expedition, lets them run into the unknown, and lets them discover that real research stands behind the game world.

2.3 Misunderstanding of scientific certainty

Simplified or overconfident claims about space are common. For example, finding a planet in a star's habitable zone is often misread as proof of life. In fact, the habitable zone alone does not prove liquid water, a suitable atmosphere, biological activity or livable conditions.

LUNARVERSE teaches players to tell apart four things:

•     Observed data

•     Calculated values

•     Scientific hypotheses

•     Assumptions and fiction

In an age of AI-generated content and information overload, separating confirmed facts from assumptions is an essential skill. The game develops not just curiosity about space, but critical scientific thinking.

3. NASA Data: The Scientific Foundation

LUNARVERSE is built on real science from NASA's research. We deliberately chose a real target rather than an invented one: Kepler-452 b, an exoplanet found by NASA's Kepler mission. The NASA Exoplanet Archive, which provides public data on exoplanets, their stars and related research, is central to the project.

3.1 Kepler-452 b

Kepler-452 b was announced in 2015 and drew wide attention because it orbits in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star. According to the published solution by Jenkins et al. (2015), it has an estimated radius of about 1.63 Earth radii, an orbital period of about 384.843 days and an orbital distance of about 1.046 astronomical units. NASA describes it as a super-Earth in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star. The system lies roughly 1,400 light-years from Earth.

There is also an important scientific nuance. The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists Kepler-452 b as a Confirmed Planet and at the same time flags it as Controversial. This reflects later scientific discussion about the reliability of its weak transit signal.

We consider this essential to the project. Instead of hiding uncertainty to tell a neater story, we make it part of the experience. A discovery is not always a final answer. Sometimes it is the start of years of checking hypotheses and revising conclusions.

3.2 Why this data matters

Scientific data is valuable not only because it tells us about a distant planet, but because it shows how hard it is to learn anything about the universe. The transit method, for example, detects a small dip in a star's brightness when a planet passes in front of it. That is how scientists find exoplanets and estimate their sizes.

This is a strong chance to turn the scientific process into interactive learning. We want players to understand not just the result, but the mechanism behind it. We shift the question from "What did scientists find?" to the more important one: "How can we know this?"

4. Relevance to the Challenge: Space Mission Design

The Space Mission Design Game challenge asks teams to build a game in which players design and manage a space mission, make engineering decisions, handle limited resources and see how their choices affect mission success.

LUNARVERSE answers this by placing the player in command of AURORA-1, where choices about what to protect, what to measure and what to conclude have visible consequences. The expedition faces limited resources and a crisis, and the player must weigh crew safety, scientific return and risk.

[Team to confirm and describe exactly what mission-design decisions exist in the submitted build, for example resource allocation, instrument choice, crisis response. If a mechanic is a prototype, say so. Judges check the description against the demo.]

The real science also supports mission-design thinking. Kepler-452 b lies about 1,400 light-years away, so any real mission could not rely on instructions from Earth, and its crew would have to decide autonomously with incomplete information. This is clearly labeled as fiction, but it makes the mission-design lesson natural: decisions are made under uncertainty, and every choice is a trade-off.

5. Why a Game?

We could have built a website, a slide presentation or an interactive encyclopedia. We chose a video game deliberately, because information a person explores and applies is experienced very differently from information they are simply told.

In traditional educational material, the user is mostly an observer who reads, watches and memorizes. In LUNARVERSE, the user is a participant. They meet the crew, watch events unfold, face unexpected circumstances and gradually discover the science behind what is happening.

We combine three elements:

1.  Entertainment: emotional story, characters, exploration, atmosphere and gameplay.

2.  Education: explanations of astronomical phenomena, scientific methods and real discoveries.

3.  Scientific literacy: the ability to read data, judge reliability and distinguish facts from hypotheses.

We do not want the educational content to feel like a lesson that interrupts the game. We want science to be a natural part of the play.

6. Story and the Human Dimension

LUNARVERSE: The Last Signal is a story about curiosity, responsibility, the unknown and the drive to explore beyond our familiar world.

At its center is the AURORA-1 expedition. Its crew is Michael, Dustin, Uncle Yura, Sarah and Estelle. The story begins with the news of Kepler-452 b's discovery and develops into a tale of exploration and unpredictable events. During the journey the crew faces a catastrophe, after which Uncle Yura disappears. His fate remains a mystery.

For us the story is more than a way to hold attention. It shows the human side of space exploration. Behind every mission are engineers, scientists, communications specialists, analysts and many others. Space exploration needs not just technology but teamwork, decision-making, risk management and the ability to act without complete information. Science explains the universe, and human stories help explain why exploring it matters.

6.1 Where reality ends and fiction begins

We will not present fiction as real events.

•     Fiction: AURORA-1, its crew, the interstellar journey, the catastrophe and the character's disappearance.

•     Real science: Kepler-452 b and its published astronomical parameters.

Keeping this boundary clear ensures the project never gives the false impression that a real expedition exists, that life has been found, or that the real surface conditions of Kepler-452 b are known. Science fiction here supports science and does not replace it.

7. What Is Innovative

The main innovation is not 3D graphics, characters or a space theme. It is combining scientific information and emotional storytelling in one interactive space.

7.1 Turning scientific data into gameplay

Scientific catalogs are normally built for search, analysis and storage. We use them as the basis for interactive narrative:

•     The orbital period explains planetary motion and the time scale of observation.

•     The planet radius lets players explore how Earth differs from a super-Earth.

•     Transit data introduces how exoplanets are detected.

•     Different scientific estimates show why scientists revise early conclusions.

•     Uncertainty becomes a reason for analysis, not a flaw to hide.

This is very different from placing scientific facts in a game menu.

7.2 Scientific uncertainty as part of the story

We want to make one of the most interesting features of modern science part of play: not everything known to humanity is finally proven. Kepler-452 b suits this well, because it has published characteristics and disputed reliability at once. This raises real questions:

•     Can a scientific hypothesis be treated as final truth?

•     What if different studies give different estimates?

•     Why do scientists use probabilities and error margins?

•     Why does absence of evidence not always mean evidence of absence?

•     How should decisions be made when information is incomplete?

The project therefore introduces not only astronomy but the method of scientific thinking itself.

7.3 A four-level evidence system

Every piece of information in the game is labeled Observed, Calculated, Hypothesis or Fiction. This turns the question of how we know what we know into a visible part of the interface. [Confirm which of these labels already appear in the build.]

7.4 Artistic design and scientific content

We chose stylized 3D graphics with cel shading. This gives the game an expressive, recognizable look that does not need photorealism, and it also helps separate artistic visualization from scientific images and observational data. Scientific value comes from the accuracy of the content, the quality of the explanation and the chance to interact with it, not only from realistic graphics.

8. Inclusivity and Accessibility

For us, inclusivity is not a separate slide. It is a founding principle of access to scientific knowledge. Space belongs to all humanity, yet opportunities to meet space science and get quality science education are unevenly distributed. Some young people have modern labs, science clubs and specialized courses. Others are curious about space but have no such access. LUNARVERSE aims to narrow that gap.

8.1 No prior training required

The game should not require any previous knowledge of astronomy, physics or programming. Players do not need to be technical students to grasp the expedition and begin exploring scientific ideas. Complex concepts are introduced gradually through clear visuals, game situations and context.

8.2 Geographic inclusivity

Talented young people live everywhere, including regions where specialized scientific resources are limited. A lack of expensive equipment or research infrastructure should not stop someone from developing an interest in space. This is why NASA's open data matters so much to us: it lets work from global research reach educational projects created far from major research centers.

8.3 Visual and cognitive accessibility

We aim for an interface that is clear to people with different levels of digital literacy:

•     Simple navigation without overly complex interface elements

•     Visual explanations of scientific ideas

•     Gradual introduction of new terms

•     A mix of text and visuals

•     Core information understandable without specialist background

Future goals, not yet implemented: multilingual support, subtitles, adjustable text display and further accessibility options. We present these as goals, not as existing features. [Move any item that is already working into an "implemented" list.]

8.4 Gender inclusivity

Space exploration, engineering, programming and astronomy should be open to everyone. Our expedition includes both male and female characters. We want to avoid presenting science as belonging to one group of people. Taking part in exploring the universe should depend on curiosity, ability and the wish to learn.

8.5 Inclusivity through open science

NASA provides scientific materials that researchers, developers, teachers, students and independent creators can use. This lets people outside the space industry take part. LUNARVERSE is an example of how the results of major scientific programs can gain a new educational and social life through independent digital projects.

9. Educational Impact

We do not aim to replace school or university astronomy courses. We aim to complement them with a new way of engaging with scientific knowledge. We see five main outcomes:

1.  Interest in astronomy. Players meet exoplanets, star systems, observation methods and current space research.

2.  Scientific literacy. Players learn to separate measurements, calculations, hypotheses and fictional assumptions.

3.  Familiarity with real sources. Science does not appear from nowhere. Behind it stand telescopes, observations, missions, publications and archives.

4.  Critical thinking. The game encourages players to ask questions, check information and not accept every claim unexamined.

5.  Interest in STEM careers. Meeting space research can be a first step toward programming, physics, engineering, data analysis and other fields.

If even some players open the NASA Exoplanet Archive for the first time after playing, become curious about the Kepler mission, or decide to study astronomy, that is already a meaningful educational result.

10. Why This Matters for NASA

NASA does more than launch spacecraft and run research. A key part of its work is widening access to knowledge, inspiring new generations and building public interest in science. NASA Space Apps exists to let people with many different skills use NASA's open data to create solutions, ideas and digital products, and participants include programmers, scientists, designers, storytellers, educators and students from many countries.

LUNARVERSE fits this goal by bringing several fields together: space science, game development, scientific visualization, educational technology, creative storytelling and the promotion of open data. We want to show that NASA data can be used well beyond traditional scientific tools, in formats that can reach new audiences. For a generation raised in a digital environment and used to learning through visual and interactive media, this matters.

11. Why Choose LUNARVERSE

Space Apps brings together thousands of participants and hundreds of projects, and many teams build impressive apps, visualizations and tools. We do not claim to be better simply because our project is about space. Here is the specific value we offer.

A different way to popularize science. Most people meet space discoveries through news, documentaries, photographs and popular articles. LUNARVERSE adds a format in which the person becomes part of a fictional expedition built on real scientific information. This can reach people who would never open a scientific catalog or a research paper on their own.

A blend of disciplines. The project sits where fields rarely meet in one small educational product: astronomy and exoplanet science, interactive development, art and visual design, science communication, and STEM education. It shows that solving hard problems does not always need a purely technical approach. Combining technology, creativity and human perception can sometimes reach further.

Uncertainty as part of the experience. Kepler-452 b lets us raise a question that matters far beyond astronomy: how should humanity treat knowledge that has not yet been conclusively confirmed? We want to show science as it really is, continuous observation, testing, debate and refinement of results.

Potential beyond the hackathon. The concept can expand with new missions, new objects, educational episodes and additional mechanics. Over time it could become a series of interactive science-fiction stories, each based on real space research, with opportunities to work with schools, youth organizations, scientific communities and independent developers. We want to create not one game, but a scalable way to turn real scientific discoveries into accessible interactive experiences.

12. Potential Social Impact

Area

Science education: More accessible introduction to astronomy

Youth: Greater interest in STEM

Open science: Wider awareness of NASA's scientific archives

Digital literacy: Stronger skills in working with information

Critical thinking: Understanding of scientific uncertainty

International audience: Access to science content regardless of country

Creative industries: A demonstration of what science-based games can do

How we will measure results (planned)

We believe the project's value should be judged by more than downloads or views. Planned indicators:

1.  Number of players who complete the science episodes

2.  Number of times science references and primary sources are opened

3.  Change in short quiz results before and after playing

4.  Number of players who become interested in Kepler and exoplanets

5.  Feedback from students and teachers

6.  Number of educational organizations interested in using the project

These are an evaluation plan, not results. [If the team runs even a small pilot before submission, report only the real number of participants and real scores here.]

13. Technology

LUNARVERSE is built in Godot 4.7.2. We chose it for building an interactive 3D environment that brings together game logic, visual effects, animation, characters and story events. [Confirm the scripting language, e.g. GDScript or C#.] The visual concept uses stylized 3D graphics with cel shading, aiming for an expressive world with its own identity rather than photorealism.

We focus on:

•     Interaction with the game environment

•     Character animation

•     Consistent story progression

•     Clear visual presentation of scientific information

•     Optimization of game resources

•     A clear interface

We use third-party assets with suitable licenses, including the Kenney Modular Space Kit (CC0), to speed up development. Scientific accuracy and artistic freedom remain two separate layers of the project. [Disclose honestly any AI tools used for code, art, writing, voice or research.]

14. Vision for the Future

We imagine LUNARVERSE as an expandable platform of interactive science stories. Instead of a single expedition, it could include new chapters based on different areas of NASA research, each introducing a separate scientific problem, mission or astronomical object. Future directions:

•     New exoplanet systems and discoveries

•     Interactive explanations of observation methods, such as a transit light-curve minigame

•     Deeper integration of open scientific data

•     Additional mission scenarios and resource systems

•     Multilingual support

•     Educational modes for schools and youth centers

•     Comparing the player's decisions with real scientific data

These are roadmap items. Our long-term goal is to make scientific research closer, clearer and more interesting to people who have never had direct contact with the field.

15. Conclusion: Why LUNARVERSE Matters

Humanity has more ways than ever to explore the universe, through new telescopes, spacecraft and scientific programs. But a discovery matters not only when it is made. It matters even more when its results become accessible, understandable and useful to society.

We believe the next step in popularizing science is not just new ways to get information, but new ways to interact with it. LUNARVERSE is our attempt to contribute to that. We want to unite what usually exists apart: scientific data, digital art, video games and human stories. We want to show young people that space science is not a closed field for professional scientists only. It is a vast world of opportunity where programmers, artists, designers, researchers, engineers and simply curious people can find a place.

Scientific progress begins not with ready answers, but with questions. What lies beyond our planet? How do we learn about worlds we have never seen directly? How reliable is our knowledge? And what is left for humanity to discover?

LUNARVERSE is not an attempt to show people what the future of space exploration might look like. It is an attempt to help them become curious about how humanity is discovering that future today.

We don't just want people to play a space game. We want them to become curious about the science behind it.
